steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on an SE(3) equivariant augmented coupling flow for Boltzmann generators. Motivate the problem of sampling molecular Boltzmann distributions, explain the gap left by existing flows, CNFs and diffusion models, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Boltzmann distribution and Boltzmann generators; symmetries and energy-based training
- Existing coupling flows on internal coordinates and their limits
- SE(3) equivariant CNFs and diffusion models and their cost
- The gap: no fast, equivariant, Cartesian Boltzmann generator
- Our proposal and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - Boltzmann distribution = equilibrium configurations of a molecule; promising for deep generative models
  - unnormalized density from physical modeling; sampling needs MD simulations: expensive, correlated samples
  - Boltzmann generators: surrogate deep generative models; independent samples, debias expectations via importance weighting
  - symmetries: rotation, translation (\mathrm{SE}(3)), permutation -> training efficiency, generalization
  - also need fast sampling and density evaluation -> energy-based training (unnormalized density)
  - energy training: model quality not limited by quality/quantity of MD samples
- Internal-coordinate coupling flows
  - bond distances, bond angles, dihedral angles; \mathrm{SE}(3) invariant
  - depend on molecular graph, non-unique for most graphs
  - struggle with interactions of far-apart nodes, no permutation invariance of some atoms -> unsuitable for particle systems like LJ13
- CNFs / diffusion
  - \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariance in CNFs on Cartesian coordinates, and diffusion models
  - built on \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant GNNs; any molecular graph -> one model across many molecules
  - but thousands of network evaluations for sampling/density -> no energy training
- Gap: no Boltzmann generator that (i) Euclidean coordinates (ii) \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariance (iii) fast sampling
- Proposal
  - flexible \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant coupling flow on Cartesian coordinates, fast sampling and density evaluation
  - augment coupling layer input with auxiliary variables acted on by \mathrm{SE}(3); project atoms into invariant space, standard flow transform, project back
  - maximum likelihood: matches \mathrm{SE}(3) CNFs, diffusion, internal-coordinate flows on molecular generation; >10 times faster sampling; concurrently with other work, first full Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide in Cartesian coordinates
  - energy-based training on DW4 and LJ13; CNFs/diffusion intractable; internal-coordinate flows lack permutation invariance -> only applicable permutation and \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant method

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Modeling the distribution of a molecule’s configurations at equilibrium, which is called the Boltzmann distribution, is a promising application of deep generative models. The unnormalized density of the Boltzmann distribution can be obtained with physical modeling, but sampling from it usually requires molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and these are expensive and produce correlated samples. A promising alternative is to use surrogate deep generative models, called Boltzmann generators. We can draw independent samples from them and debias any expectations estimated with the samples using importance weighting. The Boltzmann distribution typically has rotation and translation symmetries, known as the Special Euclidean group \mathrm{SE}(3), and also permutation symmetry. It is important to incorporate these constraints into the model because they improve training efficiency and generalization. Other key desiderata of Boltzmann generators are fast sampling and fast density evaluation. These are needed for energy-based training, which means training with the unnormalized density of the Boltzmann distribution. Training by energy is critical because then the model quality is not constrained by the quality and quantity of MD samples.

The existing coupling flows that approximate the Boltzmann distribution of molecules are at least partially defined over internal coordinates, i.e. bond distances, bond angles, and dihedral angles, which are \mathrm{SE}(3) invariant. But how these are defined depends on the molecular graph, and for most graphs they are non-unique. Also, models parameterized in internal coordinates have trouble capturing interactions among nodes that are far apart in the graph, and they cannot capture the permutation invariance of some atoms. So they are not suitable for particle systems such as LJ13. \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariance constraints have been applied to continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) that operate on Cartesian coordinates, and to diffusion models, which are closely related. These models are built on \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs). These architectures can be applied to any molecular graph, so a single generative model can generalize across many molecules. However, sampling from and evaluating the density of CNFs and diffusion models usually needs thousands of neural network evaluations, and this prevents training them by energy. So at the moment there is no Boltzmann generator that (i) acts on Euclidean coordinates of atoms (ii) enforces \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariance, and (iii) allows for fast sampling.

To fill this gap, we propose a flexible \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant coupling flow which operates on the Cartesian coordinates of atoms and allows fast sampling and density evaluation. Our contributions are:

- We make coupling layers \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant by augmenting their input space with auxiliary variables that \mathrm{SE}(3) can act on. We update the atom positions conditioned on the auxiliary variables: first we project the atoms into an \mathrm{SE}(3) -invariant space, then we apply a standard normalizing flow transform, and then we project its output back onto the equivariant space.

- We show that when it is trained by maximum likelihood, our flow matches the performance of existing \mathrm{SE}(3) CNFs and diffusion models, and also of coupling flows operating on internal coordinates, on molecular generation tasks. Sampling from our flow is more than 10 times faster than from \mathrm{SE}(3) CNFs and diffusion models. Concurrently with other work, we are the first to learn the full Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide only in Cartesian coordinates.

- We show our flow in the energy-based training setting on DW4 and LJ13, where the parameters are learned only from the molecular energy function. Energy-based training of CNFs or diffusion models is intractable because sampling and density evaluation are slow. Flows operating on internal coordinates cannot capture the permutation invariance of these problems. So our flow is the only existing permutation and \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant method that can tractably be applied there.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Modeling the distribution of a molecule’s configurations at equilibrium, known as the Boltzmann distribution, is a promising application of deep generative models [1]. While the unnormalized density of the Boltzmann distribution can be obtained via physical modeling, sampling from it typically requires molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which are expensive and produce correlated samples. A promising alternative is to rely on surrogate deep generative models, known as Boltzmann generators, from which we can draw independent samples and debias any expectations estimated with the samples via importance weighting. The Boltzmann distribution typically admits rotation and translation symmetries, known as the Special Euclidean group \mathrm{SE}(3), as well as permutation symmetry. These constraints are important to incorporate into the model as they improve training efficiency and generalization [2,3,4]. Other key desiderata of Boltzmann generators are fast sampling and density evaluation, which are necessary for energy-based training, that is, training using the Boltzmann distribution’s unnormalized density [1,5,6]. Training by energy is critical, as it prevents the model quality from being constrained by the quality and quantity of MD samples.

Existing coupling flows which approximate the Boltzmann distribution of molecules are at least partially defined over internal coordinates, i.e. bond distances, bond angles, and dihedral angles [7,8,9,6], which are \mathrm{SE}(3) invariant. However, their definition depends on the molecular graph, and they are non-unique for most graphs. Furthermore, models parameterized in internal coordinates struggle to capture interactions among nodes far apart in the graph and cannot capture the permutation invariance of some atoms, making them unsuitable for particle systems such as LJ13 [4]. \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariance constraints have been applied to continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) operating on Cartesian coordinates [4,10], and to the closely related diffusion models [11,12,13]. These models are built upon \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs) [14,15,3], architectures which can be applied to any molecular graph [16], enabling a single generative model to generalize across many molecules. Unfortunately, sampling and evaluating the density of CNFs and diffusion models typically requires thousands of neural network evaluations [17], preventing them from being trained by energy. As such, presently no Boltzmann generator exists that (i) acts on Euclidean coordinates of atoms (ii) enforces \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariance, and (iii) allows for fast sampling.

To address this gap, we propose a flexible \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant coupling flow that operates on the Cartesian coordinates of atoms and allows for fast sampling and density evaluation. Our contributions are:

- We extend coupling layers to be \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant by augmenting their input space with auxiliary variables [18] which can be acted upon by \mathrm{SE}(3). We update the atom positions conditioned on the auxiliary variables by first projecting the atoms into an \mathrm{SE}(3) -invariant space, then applying a standard normalizing flow transform, and finally projecting its output back onto the equivariant space.

- We demonstrate that, when trained by maximum likelihood, our flow matches the performance of existing \mathrm{SE}(3) CNFs and diffusion models, as well as coupling flows operating on internal coordinates, on molecular generation tasks. Our flow is more than 10 times faster to sample from than \mathrm{SE}(3) CNFs and diffusion models. Concurrently with [19], we are the first to learn the full Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide solely in Cartesian coordinates.

- We demonstrate our flow in the energy-based training setting on DW4 and LJ13, where parameters are learned using only the molecular energy function. Energy-based training of CNFs or diffusion models is intractable due to slow sampling and density evaluation, and flows operating on internal coordinates are not able to capture the permutation invariance of these problems. Hence, our flow is the only existing permutation and \mathrm{SE}(3) equivariant method that can tractably be applied there.
